Validate predicted treatment effects

Source: R/validate_benefit.R
validate_benefit.Rd

This experimental internal function is under development and issues a warning when called. It is not called by catecv(). Summarize calibration of predicted treatment effects and the population effect of a treatment rule using independent validation data.

Usage

validate_benefit(
  y,
  trt,
  benefit,
  groups = 5,
  threshold = 0,
  higher.y = TRUE,
  propensity = NULL
)

Arguments

y

Numeric observed binary or continuous outcome.

trt

Numeric treatment assignment, coded 0 for control and 1 for treatment.

benefit

Numeric predicted treatment effect for each participant, on the outcome difference scale (treatment minus control).

groups

Positive integer number of quantile groups for calibration. Tied predictions are kept together, so fewer groups may result.

threshold

Numeric treatment-effect threshold on the same scale as benefit. Treatment is recommended when predicted benefit exceeds it.

higher.y

Whether larger outcomes are desirable. If FALSE, the treatment rule recommends treatment when the predicted difference is less than threshold. Effects are still reported as treatment minus control.

propensity

Optional numeric vector of treatment probabilities, one per participant, strictly between 0 and 1. If supplied, inverse probability weighting is used; if NULL, unadjusted arm means are used.

Value

A list with mean.bias (observed treatment difference minus mean prediction), calibration (group sizes, arm counts, mean predictions, observed differences and standard errors), calibration.fit (group-level intercept, slope, R-squared and RMSE), and policy (rule treatment proportion and outcome differences for the rule versus its opposite, control for all, and treatment for all). Policy differences are oriented so positive values indicate better outcomes under the rule.

Details

Unadjusted estimators assume randomized treatment assignment with a common, positive probability of each treatment. With propensity scores, identification requires conditional exchangeability given the treatment-model covariates, positivity and a correctly specified treatment model. Both approaches require consistency and no interference for causal interpretation. Predictions should be obtained from independent data or appropriate cross-validation. Censoring and treatment costs are not adjusted for. A threshold changes the treatment rule, but policy results remain outcome differences and do not subtract treatment costs.

Calibration groups are formed from empirical quantile cut points; ties are never split. Group summaries are differences in arm means, using normalized inverse probability weights when propensity scores are provided. The fitted line and RMSE give equal weight to each group and describe group-level approximations, not individual treatment effect prediction error. A group lacking either treatment arm has an unavailable observed difference; in that case the calibration fit is unavailable. The policy estimates standardize arm-specific outcomes within the two rule categories to their observed proportions, allowing unequal randomization probabilities. A required empty treatment arm makes the corresponding policy result unavailable. Unadjusted standard errors require at least two observations in each arm. Weighted standard errors are unavailable: uncertainty in estimated treatment models is not accounted for by the unadjusted formula. Truncated or misspecified propensity scores can bias weighted estimates.

References

Hoogland et al. (2021), doi:10.1002/sim.9154 ; Efthimiou et al. (2023), doi:10.1002/sim.9665 .
